value: Study analyzed 6,874 publicly available metagenomes from 36 datasets across 25 countries and 6 continents
Reconstructed 1,023 high-quality P. copri genomes (17 isolates, 1,006 MAGs)
P. copri is 39.1% prevalent in healthy individuals from current metagenomic profiles
P. copri is often the most abundant species identified when present (34% of instances)
Ancient metagenomes from 5,300-year-old Iceman and pre-Columbian Mexican coprolites (1,300±100 BP) analyzed
P. copri clade divergence estimated to have begun 6.5 million years ago (split of clade B)
Clade A, D, and C diversification estimated between 3.5-2.5 million years ago
Within-clade differentiation relatively recent, following emergence of Homo sapiens circa 315 ka
Family transmission: same strain identified in 5 of 26 cases (19.2%) among family members
Multi-generational dietary modifications proposed as driving factor for reduced prevalence in Westernized populations
uncurated_metadata.evidence_quote: we performed an analysis of 6,874 publicly available metagenomes from 36 individual datasets
uncurated_metadata.notes: Additional contextual information about study design, sample sizes, and key findings not fitting other schema fields.

host_species.evidence_quote: Prevotella copri is a common human gut microbe; intestinal microbiome
host_species.notes: Study focuses on P. copri in the human gut microbiome. Study participants included healthy individuals and patients from Ghana, Ethiopia, Tanzania, and ancient human samples.

This paper is a large-scale metagenomic population genetics study of Prevotella copri across multiple cohorts and continents. The newly sequenced cohorts (Ghana, Tanzania, Ethiopia) consist of healthy individuals only. The schema fields largely concern individual-level clinical and phenotypic data (pregnancy, birth weight, treatment response, etc.), which are not the focus of this microbiome composition study. Most fields are correctly reported as 'not_reported' because the paper does not measure or report individual clinical phenotypes beyond basic demographics (age, sex) and health status (healthy). The paper includes analysis of publicly available metagenomic datasets with disease phenotypes (CRC, T2D, IBD, etc.), but individual-level disease or treatment data are not provided in the supplied text.

This paper is a population genomics and metagenomic study of Prevotella copri, not a clinical disease outcome study. Extracted data reflect microbiological and genetic measurements rather than patient health outcomes.

The study involved multiple geographic and lifestyle populations (Westernized vs. non-Westernized) but did not stratify results by these subgroups in a way that would warrant subgroup-level extraction; prevalence and abundance data are reported as comparisons between populations rather than as distinct cohort-level summaries.
